tests.name: weather-cli commits
todo-api commits via stdin
photo-sorter unprefixed commits

checks.rule: Find the tag and list commits since it; classify them
checks.evidence: Session ran `git tag && git log --oneline v1.0..HEAD`. The user named v1.0, so the skill uses it. The skill's script and log steps give the same commit list.

checks.rule: Title `# Release Notes` and `## What's new since <tag>`, with no invented version or date
checks.evidence: Accepted file used `# Release Notes` and `## Changes since v1.0`, with no version or date. The skill's heading wording differs slightly, which is a formatting difference the user wouldn't care about.

checks.rule: Sections in order and only when non-empty (Security first, then New features, Improvements, Bug fixes, Documentation)
checks.evidence: Accepted output has New features, Bug fixes and Documentation. The empty Security and Improvements sections are omitted, as the skill requires.

checks.rule: Write for end users with bold feature names and flags in backticks
checks.evidence: Accepted bullets: "**Choose your units.** A new `--units` flag…" and "**Multi-day forecasts.** Use `--days`…".

checks.rule: Omit internal-only changes (refactor, chore, tests); omit dependency bumps unless users would notice
checks.evidence: The accepted notes leave out the refactor and the pytest 8.3 bump, matching the skill.

checks.rule: If commits only touch CHANGES.txt, rely on the messages
checks.evidence: The diff stat shows only CHANGES.txt changed. The session wrote the notes from the commit messages and said so in its reply.

checks.rule: One-line reply: file saved, what was covered, what was left out, and that a version number must be added
checks.evidence: The session's one-sentence reply covers the file, the contents and the omissions. The skill adds a version-number reminder, which is harmless and consistent with the user's one-line request.

judged.reason: Following the skill would produce essentially the accepted output. The content, section selection, omissions and one-line reply all match. The only differences are the heading wording and a version-number reminder in the reply, and neither is likely to bother the user.

checks.rule: Security section always first
checks.evidence: Note: 'put security fixes first'; the skill mandates Security first, fixing the draft's order (Security came after Bug fixes).

checks.rule: Omit internal-only changes (CI, tests, refactor)
checks.evidence: Commits 'ci: cache pip downloads' and 'test: add tests for tag filter' are omitted, matching the note.

checks.rule: Omit dependency upgrades unless users would notice them
checks.evidence: The draft listed the FastAPI upgrade under 'Under the hood'; the note asks to leave it out. A silent fastapi bump has no user-visible effect, so the skill omits it.

checks.rule: Only the allowed sections, in order (no 'Under the hood')
checks.evidence: The skill's section list has no 'Under the hood', so that section is dropped, as the note wants.

checks.rule: Say what to do when behaviour changes (500-char limit)
checks.evidence: The draft's 'shorten them to 500 characters or fewer' fits the rule and stays in the output.

checks.rule: Do not invent a version number or date; title and heading format
checks.evidence: The draft used '# Release Notes' and '## What's new since v1.0' with no version number.

checks.rule: One-line reply: file saved, what was covered, what was left out, and a version number must be added
checks.evidence: The user asked for a one-line reply, and the final message follows this pattern. The skill's version would no longer mention the dependency upgrade as covered.

checks.rule: Use the user-named tag and the helper script
checks.evidence: The user named v1.0, so step 1 is satisfied. The classifier script is only a helper, so the commit set is the same either way.

judged.reason: Following the skill would give the corrected behaviour. Security comes first, and the dependency upgrade, CI and test commits are omitted. The 500-character limit gets its user action, and the version number is not invented. The one-line reply format is also compatible with what the user asked for.

checks.rule: Use the user-named tag (v1.0) and header '## What's new since v1.0', no invented version/date
checks.evidence: Accepted file has '# Release Notes' / '## What's new since v1.0' with no version/date.

checks.rule: Sections ordered, only non-empty (Security omitted when none)
checks.evidence: Accepted has New features, Improvements, Bug fixes only; no security commits exist.

checks.rule: Omit internal-only changes (rename, CI)
checks.evidence: Accepted left out 'internal: rename sorter.py to core.py' and 'Update CI image'.

checks.rule: Write for end users, bold feature name, flags in backticks
checks.evidence: '**`--dry-run` option**: preview which files would be moved...'

checks.rule: Speed-up goes under Improvements by user benefit
checks.evidence: '**Faster scanning**: large folders are now scanned about 3x faster.' under Improvements.

checks.rule: One-sentence reply: file saved, covered, left out, and note that version must be added
checks.evidence: Accepted reply is one sentence covering file, items and omissions; the skill's extra 'version number must be added' clause is a minor addition the user would not likely object to.

judged.reason: The skill's rules match the accepted output: correct tag, section structure, omission of internal commits, user-benefit wording, and a one-sentence reply. The only difference is a mention that the version number must be added, which is minor.
